## Telemedicine and the right to health: A neurosurgical perspective

Philipp Lassar´en a,b,*,1, Ishaan A. Tewarie b,c,d,1, Jakob V.E. Gerstl b,e, Jeffrey E. Florman e, Timothy R. Smith b,f, Marike L.D. Broekman b,c,g,h

Keywords: Telemedicine AAAQ Right to health Neurosurgery Ethics

A B S T R A C T

Neurosurgical task force is limited and unevenly distributed. Telemedicine has become increasingly popular, and could help neurosurgical centers meet patient right to care. This scoping review aims to evaluate the impact and feasibility of telemedicine on the right to neurosurgical care, using the AAAQ toolbox. The AAAQ toolbox consists of Availability, Accessibility, Acceptability and Quality. Neurosurgical availability is limited by the number of neurosurgeons, but by using task shifting and -sharing via telemedicine, the number of patients receiving neurosurgical care could increase without increasing the number of neurosurgeons. Telemedicine can improve geographic accessibility to neurosurgical care, but may also introduce technological literacy barriers. Acceptability of telemedicine is a double-edged sword; while a useful service, telemedicine also creates ethical concerns regarding privacy and confidentiality. Regulations and adaptations for vulnerable patient groups are key considerations for deploying telemedicine. Finally, there is emerging evidence that the quality of remote neurosurgical diagnostics and care can keep high standards. Overall, telemedicine has the potential of taking neurosurgery one step closer to meeting patient right to health, globally.

## 1. Introduction

Telemedicine, defined as “the remote diagnosis and treatment of patients via telecommunications” [1], has become increasingly popular since the coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic [2]. Within the neurosciences, telemedicine was introduced in the nineties with pro­ grams such as telestroke [2]. Technology and its integration in health­ care have continuously progressed since. Telemedicine can reduce travel costs, improve access to subspecialists, and decrease time to treatment for patients in acute and remote settings [3]. Hence, it could improve access to care and help alleviate the skewed distribution of neurosur­ gical services.

While the right to health is part of the World Health Organization (WHO) constitution [4], the complex nature of neurosurgery has resul­ ted in an uneven distribution of neurosurgical services. As of 2019, 33 countries had zero neurosurgeons [5]. Moreover, in-country distribution of neurosurgeons is often uneven, where metropolitan areas with aca­ demic centers normally host neurosurgical centers [6]. Hypothetically, telemedicine provides an attractive option to reduce these geographic and often socioeconomic constraints of conventional healthcare. In order to examine whether a new healthcare facility meets the patients’ right to care, the AAAQ toolbox is often used. AAAQ stands for Availability, Accessibility, Acceptability and Quality. The toolbox was developed by the Danish Institute for Human Rights [7], and is

Based on a multi-stakeholder approach, it aims to ensure that the minimum requirements of a sustainable healthcare system are met by the state, private actors and civil society [7]. This study aims to review the impact and feasibility of telemedicine on the right to neurosurgical care by using the AAAQ toolbox.

## 2. Methods

A scoping review of the telemedicine literature was carried out, with a focus on ethical and legal aspects. Subsequently, a qualitative analysis was performed with respect to the right to neurosurgical care using the AAAQ toolbox (Table 1) [7,8]. In the following sections, each element is discussed with a focus on relevant ethical and legal issues.

## 3. Availability

The first element of the AAAQ toolbox is availability, defined as the number and range of healthcare services provided [8]. Currently, the existence of neurosurgical care is determined pri­ marily by the presence of neurosurgical facilities. While the total num­ ber of consultations at neurosurgical centers often increases over time, telemedicine could allow for a more rapid increase. Although parts of Africa still have low internet access, the African Union and the World Bank aim to connect every African individual by 2030 through the “Digital Moonshot for Africa” project [9]. Therefore, the technological constraints on increasing the number of neurosurgical consultations through telemedicine are comparatively low. Instead, these are largely limited by the number of neurosurgeons available. Promising telemedicine alternatives include task-shifting and -sharing. Task-shifting means that less qualified staff perform tasks autonomously, and task-sharing means that highly qualified staff share responsibility with less qualified staff [10]. Good outcomes can be achieved for example when general surgery residents perform emer­ gency trauma procedures with remote guidance by neurosurgeons [10]. This concept could increase neurosurgical productivity, and hence availability, without the need of increasing the number of neurosurgeons.

## 4. Accessibility

The second element of the AAAQ toolbox is accessibility, defined as having physically, financially, socially, and administratively accessible healthcare services to everyone with information available for everyone without discrimination [8]. The essence of telemedicine is removing geographic barriers through remote services. While access to care can greatly be improved with telemedicine, digitized neurosurgical expertise crossing borders can create unique challenges. Institutions may find themselves with more competition and patients may need to choose their healthcare provider. Whereas this will increase patient autonomy, patient choice is a complex and sometimes irrational process, often involving factors outside of the patient’s direct control, such as socioeconomic status, health literacy,

and previous experiences [11]. Furthermore, the need to make the “right” choice of provider could lead to emotional distress for the already vulnerable patient [12]. Telemedicine also changes the economic circumstances contributing to patient access. Virtual consultations are likely more cost-effective by lowering the need for physical space and travel [2]. This improved accessibility may paradoxically challenge convenience and lowered costs by increasing demand in already strained healthcare environments [13]. Telemedicine integration also shifts the barriers of accessibility from geographic to technological, requiring a delicate judgement of cost to the individual patient. Other spheres of accessibility are relevant to consider as impacted by telemedicine’s integration into neurosurgery within social, administra­ tive, and informational domains. While there is the risk of exacerbating health disparities [14], benefit is often realized. For example, telestroke, a program designed for remote interaction with stroke specialists aided by local staff, has successfully improved outcomes for stroke patients at large distances from a hospital, thereby decreasing the urban–rural healthcare gap and improving distributive justice [2]. Neurosurgery can also be made more accessible through de­ velopments such as telesurgery. An early landmark of telesurgery was the transatlantic robot-assisted cholecystectomy, performed in 2001, on a patient in France by surgeons in the United States, setting the stage for global surgical collaboration [15]. However, globalization is limited by availability of technologies, licenses, clinical privileges, and cre­ dentialing [16]. These are difficult to widen as quality-of-care needs to be assured. Although such dramatic embodiments such as remote sur­ gery have not been realized substantively for these reasons, the spec­ trum of opportunity is broad.

## 5. Acceptability

Acceptability of the AAAQ toolbox is concerned with social and personal aspects of care with focus on respect for the culture of in­ dividuals, minorities and communities. This also includes maintaining ethical standard [8]. Telemedicine has been developed in the information age, and the acceptability of its services can be modeled by the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT) [17]. The UTAUT model has contributed widely by the prediction of technology adoption to the implementation of information technology and systems in fields ranging from at-home telehealth services [18] and Enterprise Resource Planning software [19]. This model has four constructs: performance expectancy (usefulness), effort expectancy (ease of use), social influence (opinion of others), and facilitating conditions (having necessary skills and re­ sources). When testing the UTAUT model on mobile health services in China [20], Brazil [21], Malaysia [22] and Bangladesh [23], all models found a significant effect of performance expectancy, but inconsistency regarding the significance of the other constructs. Interestingly, there was no digital divide between generations X, Y, and Z [21]. However, technology anxiety and resistance to change have been shown in the elderly population [23]. The aggregate results of studies on acceptability of telemedicine indicate that mobile health services should be made as useful as possible to maximize performance expectancy. As telemedicine fundamentally changes the setting of non-operative aspects of neurosurgical care delivery, patient autonomy becomes a key consideration [24]. When proposing a consultation, the healthcare providers should ensure an informed patient decision to have a remote consultation. This is particularly important as there is a general pref­ erence toward telemedicine among physicians [25]. However, patient interest should always prevail over physician interest. Healthcare communities cannot assume that a stable internet connection and access to medical telehealth devices ensure effective implementation [24]. Moreover, healthcare systems cannot assume that every patient is familiar with telehealth medical devices [24]. Remote consults may also have minor shortcomings in subtle and non-verbal communication [26],

potentially jeopardizing patient understanding of the implications of a therapy, as well as the physician appreciation of the patient wishes and needs. However, telemedicine could potentially empower patient au­ tonomy by reinforcing self-care and self-management for patients [24]. Further, telemedicine could introduce patients as active participators in their health management, empowering patients to gain awareness and influence health-decisions. Appropriate patient training and education programs have been demonstrated to offset these potential downsides [24], and should be in place for successful implementation. Privacy and confidentiality are other aspects of acceptability that need to be considered when integrating telemedicine into neurosurgery. The physical space of the patient or doctor and the transferring and storage of medical information need careful consideration. It may be difficult to keep privacy in some resource-limited and dense commu­ nities, particularly with shared technology [27]. Additionally, patients fear that their confidential conversation risk being recorded, saved, searchable and retrievable online [28]. It is noteworthy, that privacy issues are not always negatively impacted by telemedicine. For example, in contexts such as sexual health, telemedicine has shown to be more efficient than traditional healthcare in keeping privacy [29]. Patient consent is often used as approval for inherent privacy risks in telehealth devices, shifting the responsibility of privacy protection to patients. This overdependence on consent forms also results in weak privacy protocols [30]. These issues have not been explored in neurosurgical contexts but finding sound strategies to assure privacy is necessary for telehealth service to gain long-term trust. Patient privacy is often protected by overarching legal frameworks and regulations; regulations have been set up in the United States that prohibit telemedicine consultations with patients using programs such as WhatsApp, Facetime or Google Hangouts. Instead, in-hospital plat­ form use has been restricted to those endorsed by the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, such as Zoom for Healthcare. During the COVID-19 pandemic, this law relaxed, allowing physicians to use the previously prohibited programs [2]. Notably, WhatsApp, the instant messaging service with most users globally, has also previously been used frequently in several countries to send patient-sensitive informa­ tion between clinicians, as there have been lacking guidelines [31]. Currently, third-party use of private data is often regulated by the de­ velopers of telehealth devices with little individual control. Regulation and advanced encryptions are important to avoid data leaks, protect privacy, empower individual control of data, and combat cyberattacks [32]. Current guidelines published by the Food and Drug Administration are mainly focused on data security rather than patient privacy, urging developers to develop security protocols for confidential data manage­ ment. Regulations and legal frameworks focusing on the individual pa­ tient are needed as telehealth applications become more integrated with the conventional healthcare environment. Lastly, conflicts of interest may arise when providers use a particular telemedicine platform [16]. Medical professionals could own parts of telemedicine companies, be employed by them, or otherwise profit from referring patients to a particular service. While scientists are expected to declare conflicts of interest, research has shown that many fail to do so [33]. There is strong legal guidance in some countries such as the United Stated that professionals should have no competing interests. Neuro­ surgery must assure the highest ethical standards for implementing telemedicine to assure wide acceptability.

## 6. Quality

Quality of the AAAQ toolbox is concerned with delivering healthcare compliant with appropriate scientific and medical standards including the necessary skills, training, supplies, and environment [8]. Neurosurgically relevant examinations are not certain to be comprehensive during telemedicine consultations but valuable lessons have been illustrated [26]. The virtual exam has been long established; more than 20 years ago, Craig et al. [34] demonstrated adequate remote

neurological assessment. Nevertheless, the remote exam focuses pri­ marily on observation rather than the established physical approach [26]. More recently, in a webinar featured during the COVID-19 pandemic by the American Academy of Neurology, the virtual neuro­ logic examination was instructed once again [35]. In terms of quality of care, potential beneficence should be consid­ ered in tandem with the aim of non-maleficence. While remote consul­ tations with neurosurgical patients may result in decisions to perform surgeries, miscommunication could potentially contradict a patient’s will. A defensive strategy would be ideal to assure high quality communication, where even the slightest doubt of the patient’s under­ standing results in an in-person follow-up meeting. Also, a request by a patient to have a telemedicine consultation should be able to be over­ ruled by the surgeon if the limitations of a remote interaction are at significant risk of compromising care. Concerns have been raised that telemedicine leads to overprescription of antibiotics or drugs taken by people with substance use disorder [16]. An American study of spine patients found increased opioid prescription during COVID-19 when telemedicine visits increased, suggesting an association [36]. In the neurosurgical context, where many patients experience pain, over-prescription via telemedi­ cine should be avoided. A follow-up analysis of prescription pattern changes of physicians and patients before and after the transition to telemedicine could serve as early signals to warn institutions about potential breaches to prescription integrity. Similar to the requirements of other novel healthcare services, tele­ medicine needs to be reliable [37]. Telemedicine platforms should correctly transmit all available information, never mix patients up and minimize interruptions during conversations. Unreliable technology has contributed to the termination of services [38]. Clinicians need to be able to communicate any concerns regarding unreliability. In the in­ ternational setting of telemedicine, a product liability system is recom­ mended, where mistakes attributable to specific stakeholders of the system should be addressed to the relevant party [39]. Failure to catch mistakes early or address them appropriately can result in both tragedies for individual patients and a long-term lack of trust for the system as a whole. Existing evidence-based guidelines should be followed with tele­ medicine, however, guidelines differ substantially between countries [40]. This creates potential legal concerns in international settings of telemedicine practice and malpractice. International actors, such as the World Federation of Neurosurgical Societies, are recommended to align best-practice guidelines. Morally, physicians are accountable for their clinical decisions. In the United States and other countries, healthcare providers also have legal liability and the precedence for providing care remotely is still evolving. In concert with these considerations and to help assure similar quality, compensation for telemedicine needs to be commensurate and respectful of in-person healthcare [3]. When policymakers, insurance companies and other stakeholders do cost-benefit analyses of telemed­ icine healthcare systems, value needs to be assessed. Key to high quality neurosurgical assessments via telemedicine is communication, completing an adequate examination and managing emotional complexity. In the neurosurgical context, studies have iden­ tified the highest benefit of telemedicine in prehospital, inpatient, outpatient and transfer triage settings [2].

## 7. Conclusions

This is the first study to review the impact of telemedicine on the right to neurosurgical care utilizing the AAAQ toolbox. Exploring each element of the framework exposes some of the uniqueness of using these technologies for neurosurgical patients. The limited availability of vir­ tual neurosurgical services worldwide follows the limited number of neurosurgeons but exposes the potential power of telemedicine. Although geographic barriers can be lessened by technology, this has yet

As telemedicine evolves, the acceptability of use in our specialty much depends on the actual usefulness of the service and the quality will always be reliant on our skills. In summary, telemedicine has the tremendous potential of taking neurosurgery one step closer to reaching the right to health, worldwide.
